Use your Shiny login with other R packages

Source: vignettes/external-integrations.Rmd
external-integrations.Rmd

An R package or database driver may need an access token before it can call a service on the user’s behalf. You can reuse the login already managed by shinyOAuth instead of asking the user to sign in again.

A connection gives your server code access to that login. Ask it for a token just before calling the other package; shinyOAuth refreshes the token when needed. In reactive server code, with auth returned by oauth_module_server():

connection <- shiny::req(auth$connection())
token <- connection$access_token(required_scopes = "records.read")
existing_sdk_read_records(access_token = token)

Replace existing_sdk_read_records() with the function from your chosen package. required_scopes lists the permissions needed for that operation. A scope is a permission name defined by the service, such as permission to read records. The other package remains responsible for sending its request.

If you are starting a new app, first follow Usage. The examples below build on that login setup.

A complete Shiny example

This example uses httr2 in place of an API client library (SDK) so you can see where the token goes. Replace the example URLs, scopes and registered callback URL with your service’s settings, and set OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET in the environment.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)

provider <- oauth_provider(
  name = "records",
  auth_url = "https://login.example/authorize",
  token_url = "https://login.example/token",
  userinfo_required = FALSE
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTH_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example/callback",
  scopes = c("records.read", "records.write"),
  required_scopes = "records.read"
)

ui <- oauth_ui(fluidPage(
  actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
  actionButton("again", "Sign in again"),
  actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
  actionButton("load", "Load records"),
  textOutput("permissions"),
  verbatimTextOutput("records")
), id = "auth", client = client)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE, refresh_proactively = TRUE
  )
  observeEvent(input$login, {
    auth$request_login()
    invisible(NULL)
  })
  observeEvent(input$again, {
    auth$reauthorize()
    invisible(NULL)
  })
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  output$permissions <- renderText({
    connection <- req(auth$connection())
    if (connection$has_scopes("records.write")) "Editing available" else "Read only"
  })

  records <- eventReactive(input$load, {
    connection <- req(auth$connection())
    data <- tryCatch({
      response <- httr2::request("https://api.example/records") |>
        httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(
          connection$access_token(required_scopes = "records.read")
        ) |>
        httr2::req_perform()
      httr2::resp_body_json(response)
    }, shinyOAuth_access_error = function(error) {
      showNotification("Authorization unavailable. Try again or sign in again.")
      req(FALSE)
    })
    list(authorization = connection$id, data = data)
  })

  output$records <- renderPrint({
    connection <- req(auth$connection())
    result <- records()
    req(identical(result$authorization, connection$id))
    req(connection$has_scopes("records.read"))
    result$data
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*")

uiPattern = ".*" lets Shiny handle the example’s /callback URL as well as the application home page.

The connection is NULL before login and after logout. Use req(auth$connection()) to wait for a login. $has_scopes() lets the app hide or disable features for which the user has not granted permission; the request must still check those permissions when it runs.

The output checks both the connection ID and permissions before displaying saved results. Keep these checks when adapting the example: otherwise data from an earlier login could remain visible after logout or a different user signs in. Clear cached results when they are no longer needed, and keep user data out of global app caches.

SDK token callbacks and database drivers

Some SDKs accept a function that supplies a fresh token for each request. Create that SDK client inside the user’s Shiny session:

sdk <- reactive({
  connection <- req(auth$connection())
  example_sdk_client(
    token = function() connection$access_token(required_scopes = "records.read")
  )
})

example_sdk_client() stands for your SDK’s constructor. Its callback keeps the connection for the login that created it. After logout or another login, create a new SDK client with the new connection.

If a database driver accepts only a token string, get the token just before opening or updating the database connection. A copied token cannot refresh itself. Follow the driver’s instructions for closing connections.

Keep tokens, SDK clients and database connections in server-side session code, away from logs, URLs and browser output. Token export does not require resource_bases. If you use shinyOAuth’s $request(), configure the API addresses it may call.

Run writes from explicit user actions, such as a button click. $has_scopes() checks the recorded OAuth permissions; the service or database still decides whether the user may access a particular row or resource.

Refresh and signing in again

By default, $access_token() looks for a token with at least 60 seconds left to live and refreshes it if necessary. Increase min_valid_for for a slow operation, or use force_refresh = TRUE when you specifically need a replacement. If a usable token cannot be obtained, the call raises an error instead of opening a login page or repeating the SDK operation.

auth$reauthorize() starts a “sign in again” flow while keeping any permissions you previously reduced with $refresh(scopes = ...). It ends the old local login; cancelling the new login does not restore it. An ordinary new login requests the client’s configured scopes again. Neither flow guarantees a password prompt or account chooser at the provider.

The module’s normal expiry and session-age settings still apply. Enable refresh_proactively = TRUE if the app should refresh before expiry. The indefinite_session = TRUE option retains an expired login for on-demand refresh, but also disables the module’s automatic maximum-age clearing; choose it only when that session policy fits the app.

Several accounts and optional profile retrieval

With oauth_connections_server(), select a saved login with auth$connection(connection_id). The resulting connection has the same methods. Use auth$reauthorize(connection_id) to replace that login. The replacement has a new ID and records the old one as replaces_connection_id in auth$connections(). Other saved logins remain separate.

If only one login is saved, auth$connection() can select it without an ID. With several, choose an ID explicitly. See vignette("multiple-authorizations", package = "shinyOAuth") (online guide).

For Microsoft tokens intended for an API other than Graph, set oauth_provider_microsoft(tenant = "organizations", userinfo_required = FALSE). This skips the Graph profile request while preserving identity-token checks. connection$identity() exposes the selected identity fields already validated by shinyOAuth. It does not fetch a new profile or prove that an API call is currently authorized.

For one login with several API tokens, see vignette("token-targets", package = "shinyOAuth") (online guide).

Advanced: connection lifetime and permissions

Call connection methods in the owning Shiny session’s reactive context. Do not serialize a connection into a worker or use it from another session. A connection and its ID survive token refresh. Logout, replacement and session closure make old references unusable, even if the same account signs in again.

Reactive expressions that read connection(), $access_token() or $has_scopes() do not rerun on token refresh alone if the login and permissions stay the same. Status methods such as $summary() can update more often. In a connection manager, automatic reads do not extend owner inactivity limits; use auth$touch() for explicit user actions.

The service may issue a token with more permissions than your app allows locally. Connection methods enforce the app’s limits, but an exported bearer token still carries all provider-issued permissions. shinyOAuth cannot restrict what another package does with that string. DPoP and certificate-bound tokens also need their configured signing key or certificate; use $request() for those tokens rather than exporting a bearer string.

Reducing permissions and replacing a login

$refresh(scopes = ...) can reduce permissions while preserving required scopes. Later refreshes keep that reduction; required_scopes on $access_token() only checks permissions and does not change them. Providers can reject a narrower request. Microsoft target tokens do not support explicit API-scope narrowing; see Token targets.

For OIDC, refresh consent (offline_access) is kept separately from the scopes reported on an access token. When explicitly narrowing, include it to retain previously requested refresh consent in later reauthorization requests; omit it to remove that request. Automatic refresh does not remove it just because a token response omits it. Refresh cannot add consent that was never granted or was previously removed.

Standalone SMART replacement logins similarly keep requested patient and encounter context. Explicit narrowing can remove optional launch/encounter context; patient context remains requested when retained patient permissions require it. See SMART on FHIR for those client profiles.

Reauthorization preserves the app’s reduced limits. A provider’s previously accepted extra permissions can remain in its token without becoming available through connection permission checks. Clients with no configured scopes continue to omit the scope request; an OIDC replacement still requests openid for its new identity check.

Advanced: asynchronous token acquisition

Use async = TRUE to obtain a promise for the token. Configure a background backend before starting the app, as described in Usage.

# Configure mirai daemons or a non-sequential future plan before starting Shiny.
# Inside the owning Shiny session:
connection <- req(auth$connection())
pending <- connection$access_token(required_scopes = "records.read", async = TRUE)
promises::then(pending, function(token) {
  # Recheck before starting work after an asynchronous boundary.
  current <- req(auth$connection())
  req(identical(current$id, connection$id))
  req(current$has_scopes("records.read"))
  existing_sdk_read_records(access_token = token)
})

An async result is a token snapshot: logout or a permission change can happen before its callback runs. The example therefore checks the current connection ID and permissions again before calling the SDK. Check them again before displaying results. Scope narrowing keeps the ID, so checking the ID alone is insufficient.

An SDK that blocks R still needs its own asynchronous request mechanism, even when token acquisition runs in the background. Concurrent async token calls coordinate their refreshes; a synchronous call does not wait for an async refresh or return a promise.

If the provider asks the app to wait before trying another refresh, shinyOAuth honors a capped Retry-After delay. A cached token can still be used if it meets the operation’s permission and lifetime requirements.

Handling token errors

Token-acquisition errors inherit shinyOAuth_access_error. Inspect error$context$reason when you want to offer a specific recovery action:

Reason Suggested response
authorization_unavailable Obtain a current connection after login.
insufficient_scope Explain which permission is missing.
refresh_pending Await async work or let the user retry later.
refresh_unavailable Try later or offer a new login.
interaction_required Offer a new login.
lifetime_unavailable The replacement token is too short-lived for the operation.
unsupported_token_binding Use $request() with the configured DPoP or mTLS transport.

Argument and configuration errors are separate. Token methods never open a login page or repeat an SDK or database operation after an error.

Advanced: background tasks and saved results

Acquire the token in reactive server code before starting an ExtendedTask (Shiny 1.8.1 or newer). Pass plain inputs and the short-lived token to the worker, not the connection, module state or refresh credential. See Shiny’s background task guidance.

# Configure future::plan(future::multisession) before starting the app.
# Inside server(), with auth already created:
load_records <- shiny::ExtendedTask$new(function(token, authorization_id) {
  promises::future_promise({
    list(
      authorization_id = authorization_id,
      data = existing_sdk_read_records(access_token = token)
    )
  })
})

shiny::observeEvent(input$load, {
  shiny::req(load_records$status() != "running")
  connection <- shiny::req(auth$connection())
  token <- connection$access_token("records.read", min_valid_for = 120)
  load_records$invoke(token, connection$id)
})

output$records <- shiny::renderTable({
  connection <- shiny::req(auth$connection())
  shiny::req(connection$has_scopes("records.read"))
  result <- load_records$result()
  shiny::req(identical(result$authorization_id, connection$id))
  result$data
})

Choose a token lifetime buffer that covers worker startup, queue delays and the operation. Acquire it close to dispatch if work may sit in a queue. A copied token cannot refresh itself, and a failed background operation is not resubmitted automatically.

The result checks prevent data from a previous login or removed permission from being displayed. Keep them even for work started by a button. Do not use cancelOutput = TRUE for this guard, because it retains the previous output. For several saved logins, check the explicitly selected connection ID.
